declarations.documentation:
An authentication failure: the token endpoint rejected the refresh-token grant (the refresh token is
revoked or expired, or the client credentials are wrong), or a Calendar API call came back 401/403 (the
access token was rejected). Retrying the same call does not help until a human re-authorizes — catch it
in a converter that escalates for re-authorization before signalling `replay.interrupted` — the run
parks as a re-authorization prompt. `message` carries the status and the
server's body.
declarations.name: auth_error

declarations.documentation:
A Calendar API call failed for a non-authentication reason: the endpoint returned a non-2xx status
that is not 401/403 (a bad request, a not-found calendar, a quota or server error). `message` carries
the status and the server's body so the model can read what went wrong and adjust. Distinct from
`auth_error` so a transient failure composes with a plain backoff retry, not a re-authorization prompt.
declarations.name: api_error

declarations.documentation:
A `watch` was wired with a poll interval WIDER than its lead window, so the gap (T+lead, T+poll)
between one poll's window and the next is covered by no window and events starting there would be
silently dropped. This is a program defect — a bad constant at the call site, not a runtime condition —
and would be a `panic` if a Katari program could raise one; since it cannot, `watch` throws this at
entry instead. `message` names both values. It is NOT a `calendar_error` (nothing failed at Google);
fix the constants rather than composing a retry around it.
declarations.name: watch_misconfigured
event
declarations.signature: data event(id: string, summary: string, start: string, end: string, html_link: string)

declarations.documentation:
A timed event's moment: an RFC3339 instant (`start.dateTime` / `end.dateTime`), e.g.
"2026-07-11T15:00:00+09:00".
declarations.name: timed

declarations.documentation:
An all-day event's moment: a bare `YYYY-MM-DD` date (`start.date` / `end.date`), with no time of
day and no timezone.
declarations.name: all_day

declarations.documentation:
Neither `dateTime` nor `date` was present — an unexpected event shape. The explicit stand-in for a
genuinely absent moment, so downstream dispatches on the variant instead of guessing from a sentinel
string.
declarations.name: undated

declarations.checkedType: agent(field: json_array | json_boolean | json_integer | json_null | json_number | json_object | json_string) -> (all_day | timed | undated)
declarations.documentation:
Classify a Calendar `start` / `end` object into the `moment` sum at the ONE parse boundary: its
`dateTime` (a timed instant) if present, else its `date` (an all-day date), else `undated`. Google nests
the moment as one of `dateTime` / `date`, so this dispatch — not a `""` sentinel test downstream — is
where timed and all-day part ways.
declarations.name: read_moment

declarations.checkedType: agent(value: all_day | timed | undated) -> string
declarations.documentation:
Render a `moment` as the string the `event` carries for the model: a timed event's `dateTime`, an
all-day event's `date`, or the empty string when the moment is genuinely absent (there is no instant to
show — the only place a `""` is honest, at the string boundary rather than as an internal sentinel).
declarations.name: moment_text

declarations.documentation:
No access token has been fetched yet. The initial `token_state`; `token_freshness` reads it as
`stale`, so the first `get_access_token` exchanges the refresh token.
declarations.name: absent

declarations.documentation:
A cached access token and the absolute epoch-millisecond instant it stops being usable (its
`expires_in` lifetime from when it was fetched, less the safety margin). `token_freshness` reads it as
`fresh` while `now < expires_at`, `stale` after.
declarations.name: valid

declarations.documentation: The classifier's verdict: a usable cached token, or none — re-exchange.
declarations.name: fresh

declarations.documentation: No usable cached token: either none was fetched, or the cached one has expired.
declarations.name: stale

declarations.documentation:
Get a usable Google access token, served by `provider` for the extent of a continuation: it returns
the cached token while it is fresh, and re-exchanges the refresh token when the cache is absent or
expired. This is the capability the tools require (`with … get_access_token`); the raw OAuth secrets
never leave the provider.
declarations.name: get_access_token

declarations.checkedType: agent(now: number, state: absent | valid) -> (fresh | stale)
declarations.documentation:
Classify the cached token against the current instant, at the ONE boundary where freshness is
decided: no token yet, or a cached token past its expiry, is `stale` (re-exchange); a cached token
still inside its lifetime is `fresh` and reused. The single `now < expires_at` comparison lives here
and nowhere else — downstream dispatches on the `fresh | stale` sum, never re-reads the clock.
declarations.name: token_freshness
declarations.signature: agent token_freshness(state: token_state, now: number) -> freshness

declarations.checkedType: agent(client_id: string of private, client_secret: string of private, continuation: agent(value: null) -> T0 with get_access_token | E1, refresh_token: string of private) -> T0 with throw[auth_error | fetch_error | parse_error] | E1 | io
declarations.documentation:
Provide the Google OAuth app credentials for the extent of the continuation, caching the access
token: `use google_calendar.provider(client_id = env.get_secret(key = "GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID"), ...)`. The
first tool call exchanges the refresh token for an access token; every later call reuses the cached
token until it nears expiry, then re-exchanges. The token cache is the provider's own state, decided by
`token_freshness`; the three OAuth secrets are captured here and submitted only to the token endpoint,
never served as a value.
declarations.name: provider
declarations.signature: agent provider[R, effect E](client_id: string of private, client_secret: string of private, refresh_token: string of private, continuation: agent(value: null) -> R with {...E, get_access_token}) -> R with E | io | prelude.throw[auth_error | http.fetch_error | json.parse_error]

declarations.checkedType: agent(value: string) -> string
declarations.documentation:
Percent-encode @value@ for an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body: the `%` escape introducer
(FIRST, so the escapes added below are not themselves re-encoded), the two characters that frame the
form (`&` between fields, `=` between key and value), and the two a form decoder rewrites (`+`, which
it turns back into a space, and a literal space). A Google refresh token or client secret can carry a
`+` from a base64 alphabet, so this is correctness, not caution. Accepted limitation: this is not a
full RFC 3986 encoder — every other character (including `/`, which is transport-safe in a form value
and is common in Google refresh tokens) passes through, which covers the credentials Google issues; the
prelude offers only literal `string.replace`, so enumerating the whole reserved set in one honest pass
is not possible here. The value stays `string of private` throughout: a pure agent applied to a secret
yields a secret, so the taint survives the encoding.
declarations.name: form_encode

declarations.checkedType: agent(client_id: string of private, client_secret: string of private, refresh_token: string of private) -> {expires_at: number, token: string} with throw[auth_error | fetch_error | parse_error] | io
declarations.documentation:
Exchange the ambient refresh token for a short-lived access token (Google's refresh-token grant),
returning the token and the absolute epoch-millisecond instant it expires. The credentials — each a
`string of private` — ride the `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body the token endpoint requires, so
this is `http.fetch` with an explicit form Content-Type, not `http.post_json`. Every failure here is an
authentication failure (`auth_error`): a non-2xx status means the refresh token is revoked/expired or
the client credentials are wrong, and a 2xx reply missing the access token is a malformed auth response
— there is no non-auth failure mode at the token endpoint, so this classification is unconditional.
declarations.name: exchange_refresh_token
declarations.signature: agent exchange_refresh_token(client_id: string of private, client_secret: string of private, refresh_token: string of private) -> {token: string, expires_at: number}

declarations.checkedType: agent(token: string) -> record[string of private]
declarations.documentation:
The `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header every Calendar API call carries. The access token is
public (the token response is declassified), so it sits in the (private-typed) header record freely.
declarations.name: bearer
declarations.signature: agent bearer(token: string) -> record[string of private]

declarations.checkedType: agent(body: string, context: string, status: integer) -> (api_error | auth_error)
declarations.documentation:
Classify a failed Calendar API response into the error sum, at the ONE boundary where the split is
decided. A 401 or 403 is an authentication failure — the access token was rejected (expired, revoked,
or scoped too narrowly) — surfaced as `auth_error`, which an attended converter can turn into a
re-authorization prompt. Every other non-2xx is an `api_error`. (403 is read as auth even though Google
also returns it for quota exhaustion; the access-rejection reading is the one worth composing a re-auth
around, and a quota 403 that is retried simply fails again.) @context@ names the call for the message.
declarations.name: classify_api_error
declarations.signature: agent classify_api_error(context: string, status: integer, body: string) -> calendar_error

declarations.checkedType: agent(value: number, width: integer) -> string
declarations.name: pad
declarations.signature: agent pad(value: number, width: integer) -> string

declarations.checkedType: agent(epoch_milliseconds: number) -> string
declarations.documentation:
Format an epoch-millisecond instant as an RFC3339 UTC timestamp (`YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ`) — the shape
Calendar's `timeMin` / `timeMax` require, produced from the epoch milliseconds `time.now` returns. The
civil date is Howard Hinnant's `civil_from_days` algorithm (a closed-form, leap-rule-correct days ->
year/month/day with no month-length tables), read in UTC; sub-second precision is dropped (the API does
not need it). Assumes a non-negative instant (post-1970, which `time.now` always is) and a four-digit
year (any realistic wall-clock instant). Pure Katari keeps the package sidecar-free; the algorithm is
validated against `Date.toISOString` across the whole range.
declarations.name: to_rfc3339

declarations.checkedType: agent(value: string) -> number
declarations.documentation:
Parse an RFC3339 timestamp back to an epoch-millisecond instant — the inverse of `to_rfc3339`, used by
`watch` to place a Calendar event's `start.dateTime` on the same numeric line as its tick's epoch window.
Reads the fixed-position civil fields (`YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS`) and folds them to days with Hinnant's
`days_from_civil` (the exact inverse of `to_rfc3339`'s `civil_from_days`), then applies the trailing
zone: `Z` is UTC, and a `±HH:MM` offset (always the last six characters Google emits for a timed event)
is subtracted so the result is a true UTC instant regardless of the event's timezone — a string compare
would be wrong, since `09:00+09:00` and `00:00Z` are the same moment. Sub-second precision is ignored (it
never affects a minute-or-coarser window). A malformed field degrades to 0 in the total-reader idiom, so
a garbled timestamp sorts to the epoch rather than throwing.
declarations.name: from_rfc3339

declarations.checkedType: agent(context: string, url: string) -> (json_array | json_boolean | json_integer | json_null | json_number | json_object | json_string) with get_access_token | throw[api_error | auth_error | fetch_error | parse_error] | io
declarations.documentation:
Issue an authenticated GET to a Calendar API @url@ and return its parsed JSON body. The one place the
`Bearer` header, the 2xx check and the error classification live, shared by `list_events` and `watch`'s
pager. A non-2xx becomes `classify_api_error(@context@, ...)` (401/403 → `auth_error`, else
`api_error`); @context@ names the caller for the message.
declarations.name: calendar_get
declarations.signature: agent calendar_get(url: string, context: string) -> json.json

declarations.checkedType: agent(calendar_id: string, max_results?: integer, time_max: string, time_min: string) -> array[event] with get_access_token | throw[api_error | auth_error | fetch_error | parse_error] | io
declarations.documentation:
Tool: list the upcoming events on a calendar. @calendar_id@ is the calendar's id ("primary" for
the user's own, or an address like "team@example.com"); @time_min@ / @time_max@ bound the window as
RFC3339 timestamps (e.g. "2026-07-11T00:00:00Z"); @max_results@ caps how many come back. Returns the
events trimmed to id / summary / start / end / link — small enough to feed straight back to the model.
declarations.name: list_events
declarations.signature: agent list_events(calendar_id: string, time_min: string, time_max: string, max_results: integer ?= 10) -> array[event]

declarations.checkedType: agent(calendar_id: string, description?: string, end: string, start: string, summary: string) -> event with get_access_token | throw[api_error | auth_error | fetch_error | parse_error] | io
declarations.documentation:
Tool: create an event on a calendar. @calendar_id@ is the target calendar ("primary" for the
user's own); @summary@ is the title; @start@ / @end@ are RFC3339 timestamps (e.g.
"2026-07-11T15:00:00Z"); @description@ is optional detail. Returns the created event (its id and the
link to open it).
declarations.name: create_event
declarations.signature: agent create_event(calendar_id: string, summary: string, start: string, end: string, description: string ?= "") -> event

declarations.documentation:
Deliver one event and record its (id, start) pair the INSTANT its `deliver_to` returns — the
per-event dedup commit. Handled inside `watch`; the pair is looked up in the durable `already_notified`
var (absent → deliver and append, present → skip), so a mid-tick failure never re-delivers an event
already delivered in the same tick. Internal to `watch`; an app does not handle it.
declarations.name: deliver_if_new

declarations.documentation:
Prune the dedup memory to @keys@ — the (id, start) pairs of the current window — dropping events that
have left it, so the memory stays bounded to one window. Performed once per tick before delivery.
Internal to `watch`; an app does not handle it.
declarations.name: retain_window

declarations.checkedType: agent(calendar_id: string, deliver_to: agent(event: event) -> null with E2, lead_time_milliseconds: number, poll_interval_milliseconds: number) -> never with get_access_token | throw[api_error | auth_error | watch_misconfigured | fetch_error | parse_error] | E2 | io
declarations.documentation:
Watch a calendar for upcoming TIMED events and deliver each one, once per activation, as it enters the
lead window — shaped like `time.watch` / `discord.watch_messages` so it composes under `parallel [ … ]`. Every
@poll_interval_milliseconds@ it lists the events whose START lies within @lead_time_milliseconds@ ahead
of the tick and calls @deliver_to@ for each not yet notified. All-day events are NOT covered (they have
no instant to place in the lead window); this watch is for timed events only.

Delivery is AT-LEAST-ONCE, exactly-once per (event id, start time) only WITHIN a single activation: an
event whose start has not moved is delivered a single time while the watch keeps running, and an event
whose start moved is a different pair, so it re-notifies. A crash-recovery restart resumes the durable
dedup memory and does not re-notify; but a replay re-run (a `replay.forever` / `replay.exponential` around the
watch re-invokes its continuation, giving a fresh activation whose memory starts empty) re-delivers every
event still inside the lead window, and a `deliver_to` failure re-delivers the events after it in that
tick on the next run. `watch` never resolves; @deliver_to@'s effects @E@ flow to the caller's handlers
unchanged.

@poll_interval_milliseconds@ must not exceed @lead_time_milliseconds@ — a wider interval leaves the gap
(T+lead, T+poll) covered by no window, silently dropping events that start there. That is a program
defect, rejected at entry with `watch_misconfigured` (a `panic` in spirit; a Katari program cannot raise
one).

No retry is built in — a poll failure (an http error, a revoked token, a `deliver_to` that throws)
propagates and kills the watch, exactly as an uncaught failure in any callee does. Compose resilience by
wrapping the watch in a replay provider (`replay.forever` for transient blips, an attended converter to
park a revoked-token `auth_error` as a re-authorization prompt). The first poll is one @poll_interval@ in (a
`time.watch` occurrence fires one interval after the start).

effects.rendered: E | io | get_access_token | prelude.throw[watch_misconfigured | calendar_error | http.fetch_error | json.parse_error]

declarations.name: watch
declarations.signature: agent watch[effect E](calendar_id: string, lead_time_milliseconds: number, poll_interval_milliseconds: number, deliver_to: agent(event: event) -> null with E) -> never with E | io | get_access_token | prelude.throw[watch_misconfigured | calendar_error | http.fetch_error | json.parse_error]

declarations.checkedType: agent(calendar_id: string, lead: number, window_start: number) -> array[event] with get_access_token | throw[api_error | auth_error | fetch_error | parse_error] | io
declarations.documentation:
List every timed event whose START lies in the window [@window_start@, @window_start@ + @lead@),
across ALL result pages — `watch`'s per-poll listing. Paginates on `nextPageToken` so a busy window is
delivered in full rather than truncated at one page. The recursion depth is the number of pages in one
poll (small and bounded — a single lead window rarely spans more than a page), not the daemon's
lifetime, so it does not accumulate like a per-tick loop would. Internal to `watch`.
declarations.name: list_window
declarations.signature: agent list_window(calendar_id: string, window_start: number, lead: number) -> array[event]

declarations.checkedType: agent(accumulated: array[event], base_url: string, lead: number, page_token: null | string, window_start: number) -> array[event] with get_access_token | throw[api_error | auth_error | fetch_error | parse_error] | io
declarations.documentation:
Fetch one page of the window listing, accumulate its deliverable events, and recurse on
`nextPageToken` until Google stops sending one. @page_token@ is `null` for the first page. Internal to
`watch`'s pager (`list_window`).
declarations.name: fetch_pages
declarations.signature: agent fetch_pages(base_url: string, page_token: string | null, window_start: number, lead: number, accumulated: array[event]) -> array[event] with get_access_token | io | prelude.throw[calendar_error | http.fetch_error | json.parse_error]

declarations.checkedType: agent(lead: number, parsed: json_array | json_boolean | json_integer | json_null | json_number | json_object | json_string, window_start: number) -> array[event]
declarations.documentation:
The timed events on one `events.list` page whose START lies in [@window_start@, @window_start@ +
@lead@) — the client-side re-filter that corrects the coarse server query. Dispatches each event's start
`moment`: a `timed` instant is parsed (`from_rfc3339`) and kept only if it falls in the window; an
`all_day` or `undated` event is dropped (the watch covers timed events only). Internal to `watch`.
declarations.name: deliverable_events
declarations.signature: agent deliverable_events(parsed: json.json, window_start: number, lead: number) -> array[event]

declarations.checkedType: agent(parsed: json_array | json_boolean | json_integer | json_null | json_number | json_object | json_string) -> array[event]
declarations.documentation:
Every event in a Calendar `events.list` reply, trimmed to `event`. A reply that carries no `items`
array (an error shape the caller already branched away from, or an empty calendar) degrades to an
empty list rather than throwing.
declarations.name: render_events

declarations.checkedType: agent(item: json_array | json_boolean | json_integer | json_null | json_number | json_object | json_string) -> event
declarations.documentation:
One Calendar event object as an `event`. Google nests the moment under `start` / `end` as either a
`dateTime` (timed) or a `date` (all-day); `read_moment` classifies it and `moment_text` renders the
string the model reads.
declarations.name: render_event
